clue.text: Measures showing vitamin in fruit

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is held inside it, so a letter goes within a word

blocks.note: B is a vitamin, used alone as a letter
plums are a fruit

explanation.surface: A dietitian's lab test checks the vitamin content of some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measures' looks like a noun for quantities but is a verb here; B goes inside PLUMS to give PLUMBS.
explanation.definitionFit: To plumb is to sound the depth of water with a weighted line, a way of gauging something.

clue.text: Small volume that has some bite

blocks.note: first meaning: an old dry measure, a quarter of a bushel
second meaning: a quick little nip, as a bird gives

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a description of a sharp cheese or wine; it is two separate meanings of one word, a capacity measure and a small nip.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names both an old unit of dry capacity and a light jab made with a beak or kiss.

clue.text: Free houseplant, wilted and missing plastic pot

indicators.note: something missing has been taken away, so those letters are removed
a wilted plant has drooped out of shape, so the remaining letters collapse into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the letters of pot, with 'plastic' saying they may sit in any order

explanation.surface: A neglected houseplant has drooped and lost its plastic container.
explanation.walkthrough: Take P, O and T out of HOUSEPLANT to leave HUSELAN, then rearrange those seven letters. 'Free' looks like an adjective (no charge) but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To unleash a dog is to let it loose from its lead, so the verb means release or liberate.

clue.text: Finance Spooner’s class stadium in the US

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words

blocks.note: a rank is a class or grade
American football stadiums are often called bowls, like the Rose Bowl
swap the opening R and B sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone is funding a first-class American sports arena.
explanation.walkthrough: RANK BOWL with its first sounds exchanged becomes BANK ROLL, run together as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To bankroll a project is to supply the money for it, so both are verbs for funding.

clue.text: A pastry poet hasn’t finished – that’s more than enough

indicators.note: something unfinished stops short, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
a bun is a small sweet baked item
Dante, the Italian poet, without his last letter

explanation.surface: A poet leaves a pastry half-eaten, having had plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: Dante, author of the Divine Comedy, is the go-to poet in crosswords; here he loses his final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Abundant describes a plentiful supply, exceeding what is required.

clue.text: Crack appearing because construction worker is bent

definitions.text: Crack appearing because construction worker is bent

blocks.clueFragment: Crack appearing because construction worker is bent
blocks.note: surface reading: a fissure opens because a labourer is dishonest or the girder is warped

blocks.clueFragment: Crack appearing because construction worker is bent
blocks.note: setter's reading: a site labourer stoops over and low-slung trousers expose his backside cleft

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' suggests corrupt and 'crack' a structural flaw; in fact it is the familiar British joke about a workman bending down and showing his bottom. Bum is British slang for backside.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the British name for the top of a workman's buttocks peeking over sagging trousers.

clue.text: Idea that’s impossible for one to get into

indicators.note: getting into something means entering it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: 'not on' is an idiom for out of the question
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone has a concept too difficult for anyone to grasp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on' is a British colloquialism for unacceptable or impossible; I slips between its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a thought, concept or belief held in the mind.

clue.text: Alternative way to ask about buying more drink?

definitions.text: way to ask about buying more drink?

blocks.note: first meaning: a different one

blocks.clueFragment: way to ask about buying more drink?
blocks.note: second meaning: the one-word question a friend asks in the pub when your glass is empty

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second meaning: the single word offered at the bar to mean 'shall I get you a refill?'
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a different or additional one, and alone it serves as a pub offer of a further round.

clue.text: Go off authority and become less liberal

blocks.note: milk that goes off is said to turn sour
a right is an entitlement or authority to act

explanation.surface: A disillusioned voter rejects official control and grows more conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' looks like rebellion against power, but it is the souring of milk.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving rightwards in politics means adopting conservative views, the opposite of progressive ones.

clue.text: Half of London at home in reserved community

indicators.note: something at home in a place is settled inside it

blocks.note: the first three of its six letters
coy means shy or reticent

explanation.surface: Half of London's population lives in a private, close-knit enclave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' suggests a booked or gated community, but it means shy here.
explanation.definitionFit: A colony is a group of people or animals living together in one settlement.

clue.text: Scandal broke but with practically nothing behind it

blocks.note: dirt is damaging gossip, as in 'dishing the dirt'
broke is slang for having no money

explanation.surface: A scandal broke, yet there was hardly any substance to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broke' reads as a verb (the story broke) but is the adjective meaning penniless; the definition imagines a bank balance with almost nothing behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirt poor means extremely impoverished, owning hardly any money or possessions at all.

clue.text: Force breezy mafiosa to become a benefactor

blocks.note: F is the symbol for force in physics
airy means light and breezy
a mafiosa is a female Mafia member; a female boss is a godmother

explanation.surface: A cheerful female gangster is pushed into doing good works.
explanation.walkthrough: Mafiosa is the feminine of mafioso, so its head is the godmother, as in The Godfather.
explanation.definitionFit: In fairy tales such a figure grants wishes and helps the heroine, so anyone generous to another is called one.

clue.text: You will be sick hearing this

definitions.text: You will be sick hearing this

blocks.clueFragment: You will be sick hearing this
blocks.note: surface reading: something so revolting it will make you vomit

blocks.clueFragment: You will be sick hearing this
blocks.note: setter's reading: words said to you because you are already ill

explanation.walkthrough: 'Will be sick' suggests nausea caused by what you hear; really it means you are unwell at the time someone offers this greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the stock wish spoken or written on cards to people who are ill.

clue.text: Surprisingly lush poetry that contains a lot of padding

indicators.note: something surprising comes out unexpectedly, so the letters emerge in an unforeseen order

blocks.note: the ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A critic finds rich, florid verse unexpectedly full of filler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Padding' looks like literary waffle, which fits the poetry, but here it is the stuffing in sofas.
explanation.definitionFit: Upholstery is the soft stuffing, springs and covering fitted to chairs and sofas.

clue.text: Single or just divorced? It could be both!

blocks.note: first meaning: not married, since getting hitched is slang for marrying
second meaning: recently released from a marriage
surface padding: a wry aside pointing out that the two meanings share one word

explanation.surface: A form asks for marital status and the answer covers two boxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It could be both!' says the one word fits either description: never wed or freshly uncoupled.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting hitched is slang for marrying, so the negative describes someone without a spouse, whether always or lately.

clue.text: Sentry abandons uniform and retreats – it’s a nuisance

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so a letter is dropped
retreating means going backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a sentry is a guard
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A soldier on watch strips off his uniform and runs away, causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: GUARD without U leaves GARD, which is then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A drag is a tedious or annoying thing or person, a colloquial term for a bore.

clue.text: English for example long for Scottish union over time

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another sits above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: lang is the Scots word for long, as in Auld Lang Syne
U is a standard abbreviation for union
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A debate about Scottish independence and how long the union with England has lasted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English' looks like the people of England, set against the Scots; it is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: English is one example of a tongue, a system of words used by a people to communicate.

clue.text: Excessively praise ingredient in mushy peas

indicators.note: an ingredient is part of a mixture, so the letters form part of the words that follow

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A food critic gushes over one component of a plate of mushy peas.
explanation.walkthrough: Mushy peas are a British side dish of mashed marrowfat peas, eaten with fish and chips.
explanation.definitionFit: To hype something is to promote or publicise it with extravagant claims.

clue.text: Woven carpets already fashioned

indicators.note: weaving interlaces threads into a new pattern, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Rugs that have been woven are ready made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woven' reads naturally with carpets, which hides that it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Precast concrete is moulded into shape before being brought to the building site.

clue.text: Flat part of silly wager will spoil the fun

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for a person who does this

indicators.note: being part of something means being included inside it

blocks.note: wet is British slang for feeble or foolish
a bet is a wager
lank hair is limp and flat

explanation.surface: Someone warns that a section of a foolish bet will ruin the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment or a level surface but means limp, as of hair. Wet as 'silly' is a British usage for feeble.
explanation.definitionFit: A wet blanket is a person whose gloom dampens everyone else's enjoyment, like a soaked cover smothering flames.

clue.text: Country that includes a huge variety of creatures

blocks.note: first meaning: a realm ruled by a monarch
second meaning: the top rank in biological classification, as in the animal one

explanation.surface: A nation boasting wildlife of enormous diversity.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface seems to describe a biodiverse nation; the second meaning is the taxonomic rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a monarch's realm and also the broadest grouping of living things in biology.

clue.text: In central Rome, clergy retain vow of silence

indicators.note: central means at the core, so only the middle letters of each word are kept

blocks.note: the two middle letters of a four-letter word
the two middle letters of a six-letter word
the two middle letters of a six-letter word

explanation.surface: Priests in the heart of the Vatican city keep their silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central' applies to all three words, not just Rome: take the middle pair from each.
explanation.definitionFit: Omertà is the Mafia's code forbidding members from talking to police about crimes.

clue.text: It displays heat from lighter magma in flux

indicators.note: something in flux keeps changing, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A volcano camera shows heat rising from paler, shifting molten rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is part of the fodder, not a link: all fourteen letters of the three words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: This technique uses infrared cameras to picture temperature differences as colours on a screen.

clue.text: These men had ideas finally to deliver objectives

indicators.note: finally means at the last, so the last letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A team of men eventually came up with plans to achieve their goals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' sounds like 'at last' in time, but it picks the last letter of each of the four words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends in the sense of aims or goals, as in 'the ends justify the means'.

clue.text: Clearance given for Crown allowance

blocks.note: the crown is the top of the head
room is space or leeway allowed

explanation.surface: Permission is granted for a royal stipend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crown' suggests the monarchy and 'allowance' a payment like the Civil List; read literally they make space above one's crown.
explanation.definitionFit: Headroom is the vertical gap above a vehicle or person, as on a bridge sign.

clue.text: What’s a common alternative to standard academic request for repeat

blocks.note: par is the normal or expected level
a don is a university lecturer, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A puzzled listener weighs up the usual polite ways to ask someone to say it again.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening phrase has a double edge: 'What?' is itself the blunt everyday alternative to this more polite word.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying it as a question asks a speaker to repeat something not heard clearly.

clue.text: Prepares to follow detective’s case, so gets off at Waterloo?

indicators.note: a case is the outside casing, so only the outermost letters are kept
following means coming after, so one piece is placed behind another

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word itself
to train is to prepare or coach

explanation.surface: An officer gets ready to take over an inquiry and alights at a London terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: Waterloo is a major London railway station, and the question mark marks it as one example; 'Waterloo' also tempts towards the battle.
explanation.definitionFit: To detrain is to leave a railway carriage, which passengers do on arrival at a station.

clue.text: Messenger getting stuck into another messenger

indicators.note: getting stuck into something means being lodged inside it, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: One courier gets tangled up with a rival courier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Messenger' appears twice; the first is the definition and the second supplies its own opening letters to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Hermes carries messages for the gods; it is also the name of a British parcel firm.
